description: Plan purpose, audience, assets and triggers; choose design tools; then build a working AR prototype.
hero_image_caption: A designer sketching a wireframe layout for a digital interactive product on paper.
content_html:
From Idea to Prototype

Creating an AR product begins not with software but with planning. Before any digital work starts, a designer must define the purpose and user requirements: what should this AR product do, and what does the user need it to achieve? A retail AR product for previewing furniture has different requirements from an educational AR product used in a science lesson — the purpose shapes every subsequent decision.

Alongside purpose, the designer must identify the target audience: the age, technical ability, and context of the people who will use the product. A product for young children needs simple interactions and clear imagery. A product for professional architects needs precision and detailed data. Getting the audience wrong at the planning stage leads to a prototype that fails its users.

Content and Assets

The content of an AR product is made up of assets. At the planning stage the designer identifies which assets are needed and checks that they are of sufficient quality. The six types of asset are: audio (spoken narration, sound effects), charts and graphs (data visualisations), hyperlinks and weblinks (connections to further information), photographs and images (still visuals), text (labels, descriptions, instructions), and video (moving footage or animation). A well-planned AR product only includes assets that serve the defined purpose — adding unnecessary media increases development time and can reduce performance.

Key Fact

The six types of AR asset are: audio, charts and graphs, hyperlinks/weblinks, photographs/images, text, and video. Each type must be chosen because it helps meet the defined purpose — not just because it is available.

Triggers, Layers and Interaction

A trigger is the signal that starts the AR experience. The designer must choose which type of trigger to use based on the context. If the product will be used indoors with printed materials (such as a museum exhibit card or a product label), a marker-based trigger is appropriate. If the experience must work outdoors at a real location without physical props, a markerless/GPS trigger is more suitable. If the experience needs to replace or enhance the look of a specific physical object, superimposition is the right choice.

When designing triggers, quality matters. A marker-based trigger image must be unique — it must have enough distinct graphical detail for the recognition software to identify it reliably. Blurred images, images with too much text, and images with too much blank space all reduce recognition accuracy and should be avoided.

Once triggered, content is presented in layers. Layers should be kept simple and named clearly. An AR product may have a single layer that presents all its content at once, or multiple layers that the user can navigate. How the user moves between layers is the action flow: a static layer presents information passively; an interactive layer responds to a swipe, a click/select, or a voice command.

Key Fact

A good marker-based trigger must be unique and contain varied graphical elements. Avoid: blurred images, too much text, and too much blank space — all three reduce the accuracy of object recognition.

Design Tools

Six design tools are used to plan an AR product. Each serves a different purpose and together they form the design documentation that guides the build phase.

A flowchart maps out the action flow of the AR product — the logical sequence from trigger to content, including any decision points or branches. This is especially useful when planning interactive layers where different choices lead to different outcomes.

A mind map is used to brainstorm and organise ideas at the content planning stage. Starting with the central purpose, the designer branches out to identify topics, assets, and audience needs. Mind maps are not prescriptive — they capture the full range of possibilities before decisions are made.

A mood board collects visual references that define the house style of the product: colour palettes, typography, image styles, and tone. Mood boards help the designer and client agree on an aesthetic direction before any assets are produced.

A storyboard sequences the user experience frame by frame, showing what the user sees at each stage of the AR interaction. It is particularly useful for time-based content such as video or narrated guided tours.

A visualisation diagram shows the overall layout of the product — how layers, assets and navigation elements are positioned in the AR view. It gives a birds-eye overview of the content structure.

A wireframe is a skeletal, low-detail sketch of the interface. It focuses purely on layout and functionality without adding colour or final imagery. Wireframes are fast to create and easy to revise, making them ideal for early design discussions with a client.

What a Prototype Is — and Is Not

An AR prototype is a minimal viable product — it is not the finished AR application. A prototype must confirm functionality (does the trigger fire the correct content?) and confirm aesthetics (does the visual style match the design documentation?). It must also have access to real data rather than placeholder content. What it does not need to do is include every planned feature — limited functionality is expected and accepted.

This distinction is important. Students sometimes try to build a fully polished product when the task only requires a prototype. The prototype’s purpose is to prove the concept works — trigger fires, layer appears, information outputs correctly — so that the full product can be developed from a solid foundation.
exam_tip_html: The 8-mark ‘create’ question asks you to sketch a design document — often a mind map, storyboard, wireframe or action flow diagram — for a given AR scenario. Marks are awarded for labelling, completeness and a visible link between your diagram and the scenario. The single biggest mark loss is leaving elements unlabelled. Write the name and purpose of every element you draw. A tidy rough sketch with clear labels always scores higher than a neat drawing with no annotations.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Planning must cover purpose, target audience, content, assets, triggers and layers before any building begins.
  • Six design tools — flowcharts, mind maps, mood boards, storyboards, visualisation diagrams and wireframes — document the content design, action design and house style.
  • A prototype confirms functionality and aesthetics with real data; it is a minimal viable model, not a finished product.

practice_questions.text:
Which design tool is most useful for mapping the logical sequence of steps a user takes through an AR experience?
A. Mood board
B. Storyboard
C. Flowchart
D. Visualisation diagram
practice_questions.marks: C — Flowchart. (1 mark for correct letter or full term.)

practice_questions.text: State one type of asset that can be included in an AR product.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark for any one of: audio / charts and graphs / hyperlinks/weblinks / photographs/images / text / video.

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by the term 'prototype' in the context of creating an AR product.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (2): States that a prototype is a working model (1) that confirms functionality and aesthetics without being the finished product (1).
Secure (2): Two of the following: not full product / confirms functionality / confirms aesthetics / has access to real data.
Developing (1): States only 'an early version' or 'a test version' without specifying what it must achieve.
Emerging (0): Vague or incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features that a good marker-based trigger image should have.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per feature, up to 2 marks. Accept: must be unique / must have varied graphical elements / should not contain blurred images / should not have too much text / should not have too much blank space / should be clear and high contrast. Each answer must be a describable feature, not just 'it must be good'.

practice_questions.text: Explain why it is important to identify the target audience before starting to design an AR product.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): Identifies that different audiences have different needs (1) AND gives a specific example of how audience affects design decisions (e.g. young children need simple interactions / professionals need precision) (1) AND uses a connective to explain the consequence of getting it wrong (e.g. a product designed without audience in mind may be too complex or too simple, meaning users cannot engage with it) (1).
Secure (2): Two clear connected points.
Developing (1): States that the audience matters without explaining how it affects design.
Emerging (0): No relevant content.

practice_questions.text: A visitor attraction is developing an AR product for a guided tour of its outdoor sculpture garden. Visitors will use their own smartphones. Sketch a design for the action flow of this AR experience. Your design should show: the trigger used; at least two layers of content; how users move between layers; and the types of information output included. Label all elements clearly.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Clear action flow diagram with all four required elements present and labelled. Trigger type is appropriate for an outdoor context and justified or implied (markerless/GPS or marker on a physical plaque). At least two distinct named layers shown. Navigation between layers clearly indicated (e.g. swipe, tap). At least two labelled information output types (e.g. text description + audio narration). Diagram is coherent — a builder could follow it.
Secure (5–6): Three of the four required elements present and labelled. Minor gaps in logic or labelling.
Developing (3–4): Two of the four elements present. Diagram present but incomplete or poorly labelled.
Emerging (1–2): Some relevant content sketched but limited labelling and missing key elements.

knowledge_checks.q: Which design tool focuses purely on layout and functionality without adding colour or final imagery?
A prototype must have access to real data. Which other two things must a prototype confirm?
A mood board collects visual references that define the _____ of the AR product, including colour palettes and typography.
A marker-based trigger must be _____ and must contain varied graphical elements to be reliably detected.
Match each design tool to its primary purpose.
right: Shows the overall layout and structure of the AR content
Sequences the user experience frame by frame
Maps the logical steps and decision points in the AR action flow

flashcard_questions.q: What is the first thing a designer must define before building an AR product?
flashcard_questions.a: The purpose and user requirements — what the product must do for its audience.

flashcard_questions.q: What planning areas must be covered before building an AR product?
flashcard_questions.a: Content, assets, trigger type, and layer structure.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the six types of AR asset.
flashcard_questions.a: Audio, charts/graphs, hyperlinks/weblinks, photos/images, text, video.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a trigger in an AR product?
flashcard_questions.a: The mechanism that causes AR content to appear — a marker, GPS location, or real object.

flashcard_questions.q: Name three things that make a marker-based trigger image poor.
flashcard_questions.a: Blurred images, too much text, too much blank space.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a layer in an AR product?
flashcard_questions.a: A digital level of content stacked on top of a trigger in the AR experience.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between a static and an interactive AR layer?
flashcard_questions.a: Static: presents information only. Interactive: responds to swipe, click or voice.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the six design tools used to plan an AR product.
flashcard_questions.a: Flowcharts, mind maps, mood boards, storyboards, visualisation diagrams, wireframes.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a flowchart show when planning an AR product?
flashcard_questions.a: The logical sequence of steps and decisions in the AR action flow.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the purpose of a mood board in AR design?
flashcard_questions.a: To collect visual references that define the house style — colours, fonts, image style.
A working model that confirms functionality and aesthetics — not the finished product.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'action flow' mean in AR design?
flashcard_questions.a: The sequence of steps a user takes moving through the AR experience.

glossary_terms.definition: A clear statement of what the AR product is intended to do and what the user should be able to achieve with it.
The individual media files — audio, charts, hyperlinks, images, text and video — that are combined to create the content of an AR product.
The mechanism that causes AR content to appear — either a marker image, a GPS location, or the detection of a real object.
The individual digital levels of content that are stacked on top of the trigger in an AR experience, each potentially showing different information or interactions.
A diagram that shows the sequence of steps and decisions a user takes as they move through an AR experience.
A working model of an AR product that demonstrates its core functionality and visual style without being the finished article.
